summary: Narrowleaf bittercress is a small plant up to two feet tall in the mustard family, with finely divided leaves. It makes lots of seeds and can fertilize itself, so a single plant can quickly become a smothering colony that pushes out native plants, possibly including early spring wildflowers. It grows in rich, moist soil along ditches, streams and floodplains, and in the dappled shade of disturbed woods.
history: Narrowleaf bittercress is native to Eurasia. In the United States it was first recorded in New Hampshire in 1916, and it now grows in at least 18 states.
seasons: Its tiny white four-petaled flowers bloom from April to June, and seeds form from early May through early July. It finishes its life cycle and dies back shortly after midsummer.

handling.text: Hand-pulling or digging young plants works if it is done before the seeds form. In New York City parks like Kissena, cutting, killing or removing plants without permission from NYC Parks is against park rules, so report it instead.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks like Kissena Park, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
